hints: Start by contrasting with discontinuous traits like blood group - if height was controlled by one gene with dominant and recessive alleles, would you expect distinct groups or a smooth range?
Think about what happens if instead many different gene loci all affect the same trait, and each dominant allele adds just a little bit to the value.
Link the idea of adding up lots of small genetic contributions to why the population shows every intermediate phenotype with no clear categories.
walkthrough:
Many genes, one trait**
Think of height or mass not as the job of one gene, but as a team effort. Lots of different gene loci all influence the same trait. This is called polygenic inheritance.

Small and additive effects**
At any one of those loci, swapping one allele for another does not switch the trait on or off. It just nudges it up or down a little. Because the effects add together across all the loci, an individual with more trait-increasing alleles will be taller or heavier, and one with fewer will be shorter or lighter.

Why a smooth range appears**
With many genes each contributing a small amount, there are very many possible combinations of alleles. That produces every intermediate value between the two extremes, so the population shows continuous variation with no distinct groups.

Final answer: Controlled by multiple genes / polygenes; different alleles at a single locus have small effects on the phenotype; effects of different genes are additive / combine to give a range of phenotypes.

hints: Remember phenotype = genotype + environment. For body mass, what outside the genes must an animal take in to build body tissue?
Think about two angles - how much food is available and how good it is, plus anything else like illness or climate that changes how much energy is used for growth.
walkthrough:
Food supply builds mass**
Body mass depends on building proteins, fats and other tissues, which needs nutrients and energy. So both the amount of food available and the quality of the diet, for example protein and vitamin content or malnutrition, will increase or limit growth.

Other environmental demands**
Any factor that alters energy intake or use also matters. Disease can reduce feeding and divert energy to immune responses, reducing mass. Temperature can affect metabolic rate and appetite, for example cold increasing energy loss as heat, also changing mass.
Final answer: Any two from: quantity / availability of food; quality of food / malnutrition; disease; temperature.

hints: In natural selection the environment is the selective agent - here who decides which animals get to reproduce and on what basis?
Think of the cycle a farmer follows: choose the best adults, mate them, then what do you do with the next generation?
Consider why one round is not enough to fix a trait like high milk yield in a herd.
For the final mark, think about repeating the selection and breeding steps over many generations to concentrate the desired alleles.
walkthrough:
Humans replace natural selection pressure**
Instead of survival in the wild deciding, the breeder decides which phenotype is valuable, for example high milk yield, fast growth or disease resistance. Only animals showing that desired characteristic are chosen as parents.

Breed the best with the best**
The selected parents are bred together so their alleles for the desired trait are combined in the offspring. This increases the frequency of those favourable alleles in the next generation.

Select again from the offspring**
Not all offspring will be equally good. The breeder examines the offspring, keeps only those that best show the desired characteristic, and breeds those selected offspring together.

Repeat to fix the trait**
The select-and-breed cycle is repeated over many generations. Each cycle concentrates the desired alleles further, so the herd progressively improves and becomes more uniform for the trait.

Final answer: Humans apply selection pressure; select parents showing desired characteristic and breed them together; select offspring with desired characteristic and breed selected offspring; repeat over many generations.
